screens.title: Designing End-to-End CI/CD Pipelines with AWS CodePipeline
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we’ll make AWS CodePipeline tangible. You will understand what an end-to-end pipeline is, why stages, actions, and artifacts matter, and how CodePipeline connects developer tools like CodeCommit, CodeBuild, and CodeDeploy into a reliable release flow. We’ll also cover how to pause for human checks with manual approval gates, extend behavior with custom actions backed by Lambda, and manage your pipeline safely as code using CloudFormation or CDK. Practically, you’ll see how artifacts flow from source to build to deploy, where IAM permissions commonly fail, and how EventBridge and SNS keep teams informed. This matters because a well-designed pipeline reduces deployment risk, enforces quality gates, and makes releases repeatable and auditable. By the end you’ll be able to sketch a multi-stage pipeline for container or static workloads, choose where to add tests and approvals, and pick an approach to represent the pipeline as code. Think about a recent deployment you managed: where would an approval or a custom scan fit into that process?

Orientation

This chapter shows how to assemble stages and actions, add approvals and custom actions, and automate pipeline definition with CloudFormation or CDK so pipelines are version controlled and repeatable.

In this lesson
Design multi-stage pipelines and integrate AWS developer tools.
Coming up
Manual approvals, custom actions, monitoring, and IaC examples.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will design, implement, and operate multi-stage CodePipeline workflows for different application types. First, you will learn to map release requirements to pipeline stages and actions so that source changes progress through build, test, and deploy steps reliably. Second, you will integrate AWS developer tools—CodeCommit for source control, CodeBuild for builds and tests, and CodeDeploy for deployments—and understand when to call out to S3, Lambda, or Step Functions. Third, you will add control points such as manual approval gates and custom actions so compliance checks and bespoke automation fit into your workflow. Finally, you will author pipelines as code with CloudFormation or CDK, enabling version control, repeatable creation, and predictable updates. Each objective links skill to outcome: for example, defining a manual approval before production reduces risk and provides an audit trail; expressing the pipeline in CloudFormation ensures the exact pipeline configuration can be recreated. Keep an eye out for common pitfalls, like misconfigured artifact names or overbroad IAM permissions, as we cover each objective with practical examples.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Focus & Assessment
screens.narratorSegment: This page makes the assessment focus explicit and highlights common mistakes to avoid. You will be expected to produce a pipeline design that demonstrates correct artifact flows between stages, a working example that integrates CodeCommit, CodeBuild, and a deploy provider, and a pipeline-as-code template that can be deployed. We will check that manual approval actions pause and notify teams, and that any custom actions correctly communicate success or failure back to CodePipeline. Common errors include mismatched artifact names between actions, missing iam:PassRole or service role permissions, and misconfigured action provider parameters. When we review your pipeline-as-code, we will look for explicit artifact stores, a defined service role for the pipeline, and stage definitions for Source, Build, and Deploy at minimum. A short hands-on activity demonstrates a static website pipeline with a manual approval gate; successful completion shows artifacts flowing to S3 and a paused approval step that requires a human to continue. These checks ensure reproducibility, least-privilege IAM posture, and a clear audit trail for production changes.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Learning Objectives — Assessment
Competency Checks
  • Design a multi-stage pipeline with proper artifact names and a defined S3 artifact store.
  • Integrate CodeCommit, CodeBuild, and a deploy provider; demonstrate a successful run.
  • Add a Manual Approval stage and show the pipeline pauses and notifies via SNS.
  • Provide a CloudFormation or CDK template that recreates the pipeline resources.
Common Pitfalls
Mismatched artifact names, insufficient IAM permissions like iam:PassRole, and missing artifact stores are frequent causes of pipeline failure.
Practical Exercise
Build a static website pipeline that deploys index.html to an S3 website bucket, then add a Manual Approval stage before production deploy.
Success Indicator
On commit, pipeline runs, pauses for approval, and after approval your S3 website updates with the new index.html.

screens.title: What is AWS CodePipeline?
screens.narratorSegment: AWS CodePipeline is a fully managed continuous delivery service that automates release pipelines, turning a set of discrete tasks into an orchestrated workflow. Think of CodePipeline as a conveyor belt in a factory: stages are inspection stations and actions are the tools that operate on the product. The Source stage places code onto the belt, Build transforms it into artifacts, Test verifies quality, and Deploy places the finished product into an environment. This conveyor analogy helps you decide where to insert quality gates: tests, manual reviews, or custom checks. A concrete example: a commit in CodeCommit triggers a Source action that produces an artifact; CodeBuild consumes that artifact to run unit tests and build a Docker image, producing a build artifact that the Deploy stage consumes to update an ECS service. A common misconception is to treat CodePipeline as a build system — it is an orchestration layer; the heavy lifting of builds and tests is delegated to CodeBuild or external tools. Key takeaway: use CodePipeline to model the high-level flow and choose specialized providers for execution. How would you break a complex release into stages so failures fail fast and tests are meaningful?

keyIdea.title: Orchestration, not execution
keyIdea.text: CodePipeline coordinates stages and actions; individual services perform builds, tests, and deploys.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › What is AWS CodePipeline?
Definition & Purpose

CodePipeline provides a visual workflow that models release processes so teams can deliver application and infrastructure changes reliably. It manages transitions between stages and passes artifacts from one action to the next.

Analogy
A conveyor belt with inspection stations: stages are stations, actions are machines performing tasks on artifacts.
Misconception
Do not use CodePipeline as a build runner; delegate builds and tests to CodeBuild or external providers and use CodePipeline to orchestrate them.
Concrete Example
Source: CodeCommit → Build: CodeBuild builds Docker image and outputs to ECR → Test: integration tests → Approval → Deploy: CodeDeploy to ECS.
Key Takeaway

Treat CodePipeline as the coordinator that ensures artifacts flow through validation and deployment steps in a predictable, auditable manner.

screens.title: Stages and Actions: Structure a Pipeline
screens.narratorSegment: A CodePipeline is composed of stages and each stage contains actions. Stages represent logical checkpoints like Source, Build, Test, Approval, and Deploy. Actions are specific tasks within those stages — for example, a CodeCommit Source action, a CodeBuild action that runs unit tests and builds artifacts, and a CodeDeploy action that updates an ECS service. One strong design principle is to place fast, failing tests earlier, so failures are detected quickly and cost is minimized. For containerized apps, build produces a Docker image and pushes it to ECR; the build stage should also run unit tests and static analysis. An integration test stage can deploy to a short-lived staging environment and run end-to-end tests before approval. A common mistake is grouping too many responsibilities into a single stage; instead, split concerns so rollbacks and troubleshooting are easier. Concrete example: Source produces SourceOutput, Build consumes SourceOutput and produces BuildOutput; configure action artifact names explicitly so the next stage can find the right input. Check your artifact names and run order when pipelines fail to transition artifacts. Closing takeaway: structure stages to enforce fast feedback, clear ownership, and reliable artifact handoff.

keyIdea.title: Split responsibilities
keyIdea.text: Design stages so each performs a single logical job and actions pass explicit artifacts to the next stage.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Stages and Actions
Pipeline Steps
1
Source
CodeCommit or S3 places SourceOutput artifact for the pipeline.
2
Build & Test
CodeBuild compiles, runs unit tests, and emits BuildOutput or image references.
3
Approval
Manual approval pauses the pipeline and can notify teams via SNS before production deploy.
4
Deploy
CodeDeploy or S3 deploys the validated artifact to the target environment.
Artifact Flow Diagram
Explicit artifact names and run order matter. Example names: SourceOutput → BuildOutput. Configure InputArtifacts and OutputArtifacts so actions can locate the correct files.
Example
A CodeBuild action consumes SourceOutput, runs tests, and produces BuildOutput which Deploy uses.
Common Mistake
Leaving artifact names implicit or mismatched often causes the next action to fail to find its inputs — always name artifacts explicitly.

screens.title: Integrating Core Developer Tools
screens.narratorSegment: Integrating AWS developer tools gives each component a clear responsibility in the pipeline. CodeCommit is the source provider; it triggers a Source action and supplies the initial artifact. CodeBuild is a build and test engine: compile code, run unit tests, produce build artifacts or container images and push to ECR. CodeDeploy is the deployment orchestrator for compute targets like EC2, ECS, or Lambda — it interprets artifacts and performs the actual switch to new versions, including blue/green strategies. A useful way to reason about them is to compare responsibilities: CodeCommit owns change tracking, CodeBuild owns transformation and verification, and CodeDeploy owns release mechanics. Concrete example: for a Docker-based microservice, CodeBuild builds the image and pushes to ECR, then produces a BuildOutput artifact containing the image tag; CodeDeploy reads that and performs a blue/green deployment to ECS. Common misconception: expecting CodePipeline to perform image builds itself; instead, configure CodeBuild with a buildspec to produce the image and artifact metadata. Key takeaway: pick the right provider for each action and make their contracts — artifacts and IAM permissions — explicit so the pipeline runs securely and predictably.

keyIdea.text: CodeCommit supplies source, CodeBuild transforms and tests, CodeDeploy executes deployments; define their artifact contracts and permissions.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Integrating Core Developer Tools
Provider Comparison
CodeCommit — Source
Hosts repository and emits SourceOutput artifact to start the pipeline.
CodeBuild — Build & Test
Runs builds and tests, creates build artifacts or container images and pushes to registries.
CodeDeploy — Deploy
Applies artifacts to compute targets and supports blue/green or in-place strategies.
Example: Docker Microservice
Source commit → CodeBuild builds Docker image, tags and pushes to ECR, produces BuildOutput containing image tag. Deploy stage uses that BuildOutput to update ECS via CodeDeploy and perform traffic shift.
Pro Tip
Include metadata such as image tag in build artifact so the deploy action can reference the exact image to run.

screens.title: Artifacts and Artifact Stores
screens.narratorSegment: Artifacts are the outputs that actions produce and that subsequent actions consume. In CodePipeline, an artifact can be source code archive, build outputs, or metadata like image tags. The ArtifactStore, often an S3 bucket, is the durable place where artifacts are stored between stages. A clear artifact naming convention is essential: specify InputArtifacts and OutputArtifacts in each action so the pipeline can route files correctly. For example, a Source action writes SourceOutput; a subsequent CodeBuild action lists SourceOutput in InputArtifacts and writes BuildOutput to OutputArtifacts. If an action cannot find its expected artifact, the pipeline fails to transition. A common mistake is forgetting to set the artifact name when skipping build stages or when using multiple actions producing different outputs. Practically, when building a static website pipeline, SourceOutput should contain index. html and BuildOutput can be skipped if no build is required; configure the Deploy action to extract files from SourceOutput. Key takeaway: artifacts and the artifact store are the contract between actions — define names and stores explicitly to avoid handoff errors. Artifacts and Artifact Stores means treat artifacts and the artifact store as explicit contracts between actions; name them clearly and use s3 as the durable store.. In practical terms, how artifacts travel between actions and the role of s3. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Artifacts & Artifact Stores
Artifact Concepts
Artifacts pass outputs from one action to the next. Use S3 as the artifact store and name artifacts explicitly so InputArtifacts and OutputArtifacts match across actions.
Example
Source action: OutputArtifacts: [SourceOutput]. Build action: InputArtifacts: [SourceOutput], OutputArtifacts: [BuildOutput]. Deploy action: InputArtifacts: [BuildOutput].
Practical Checkpoints
  • Confirm artifact names match exactly between action definitions.
  • Ensure pipeline ArtifactStore references a valid S3 bucket.
  • When skipping build steps, point Deploy to SourceOutput if it contains deployable files.
Common Mistake
Mismatched artifact names cause a silent failure to find inputs and stop the pipeline from progressing.

screens.title: Extending Pipelines with S3, Lambda, and Step Functions
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond the core developer tools, CodePipeline integrates well with S3, Lambda, and Step Functions to handle artifact storage, custom logic, and long-running orchestration. Use S3 as an artifact store and also as a deploy target for static websites. AWS Lambda commonly implements custom actions: a Lambda function can run a proprietary security scan, manipulate artifacts, or emit success and failure back to CodePipeline. Step Functions are useful when a pipeline needs to coordinate a sequence of longer-running tasks or multiple Lambda calls as part of a single logical action. For example, a SecurityScan stage might invoke a Step Functions workflow that executes several scanners and aggregates results; that workflow can then return status to CodePipeline via a custom action. A common misconception is to overuse Lambda for heavy compute; keep Lambdas lightweight and prefer CodeBuild or Step Functions for heavier workloads. When integrating these services, define clear input and output contracts and ensure the pipeline role and any invoked roles have least-privilege permissions. Takeaway: use S3 for durable artifacts, Lambda for short custom actions, and Step Functions when you need orchestrated, multi-step custom logic.

keyIdea.text: S3 stores artifacts, Lambda enables custom actions, and Step Functions orchestrate complex multi-step custom work.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Extending with S3, Lambda & Step Functions
Integration Patterns
S3: artifact store and static website target.
Lambda: implement custom actions that signal success or failure back to CodePipeline.
Step Functions: orchestrate multi-step custom workflows invoked by a custom action.
Misconception
Avoid running heavy compute in Lambda; for sustained compute use CodeBuild or Step Functions with larger compute resources.
Example: Security Scan
Create a custom action that triggers a Lambda which starts a Step Functions workflow to run multiple scanners. The workflow aggregates results and the Lambda calls PutJobSuccessResult or PutJobFailureResult to notify CodePipeline.
Key Takeaway
Extend pipelines with the right AWS service for the job and keep clear contracts for inputs, outputs, and permissions.

screens.title: Manual Approval Gates
screens.narratorSegment: Manual approval gates insert human judgment into an automated pipeline. You add an Approval action in a stage and when the pipeline reaches that action it pauses until an authorized user reviews and approves or rejects progression. Approvals are essential for production deployments, compliance checks, and high-risk releases. In practice you pair an approval action with SNS notifications so the right people know a review is required and have links to artifacts or logs to make their decision. A concrete example: after an integration test stage you add a ManualApproval action that references an SNS topic; reviewers receive a notification, examine test reports or artifacts, and then approve the pipeline to proceed to production. Misconception: approvals are not a substitute for automated tests — they are complementary and should follow meaningful automated validation so reviewers are not forced to manually validate trivial failures. Practical tip: limit who can approve by IAM and include a clear review checklist in the approval message. Closing question to reflect on: which release types in your organization require manual approval, and what evidence should reviewers see before approving?

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Manual Approval Gates
Why Approvals?
Approvals give teams a controlled pause before sensitive operations, ensuring compliance and human oversight.
Practice
Add an Approval action and optionally attach an SNS topic so reviewers receive notifications and a link to artifacts for inspection.
Checklist for Reviewers
  • Confirm automated tests passed and required security scans ran.
  • Examine artifact metadata and release notes.
  • Verify IAM and runtime configuration for production deployment.
Key Takeaway
Use approvals sparingly for high-risk steps and always provide reviewers with concise evidence to make fast, informed decisions.

screens.title: Custom Actions and Lambda Integration
screens.narratorSegment: Custom actions let you plug functionality into a pipeline that CodePipeline does not natively support. To build a custom action you define an action type and implement the action logic, typically in a Lambda function or an agent running on EC2. The custom action must communicate back to CodePipeline by calling PutJobSuccessResult or PutJobFailureResult so the pipeline knows whether to proceed. A practical scenario is a proprietary security scanner: you might have a SecurityScan stage that uses a custom action; the Lambda invokes the scanner, waits for results, then signals pass or fail. A common pitfall is not handling timeouts or long-running scans: if the scan takes minutes, ensure the Lambda design or execution model supports waiting or that Step Functions are used to orchestrate extended work. Misconception: custom actions are a free-form replacement for tests — they are best used when a tool cannot be integrated as a standard provider. Key takeaway: implement clear success/failure signaling and robust error handling in custom actions, and ensure the pipeline role and any invoked roles have only the permissions required for the task.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Custom Actions & Lambda
Custom Action Pattern
Define a custom action type and implement the execution logic. Use Lambda or an agent to perform the work and call PutJobSuccessResult or PutJobFailureResult.
Example
A proprietary scanner runs in Lambda, produces a report in S3, and signals CodePipeline with success or failure depending on findings.
Design Considerations
  • Handle long-running tasks using Step Functions or asynchronous patterns.
  • Ensure invoked roles have least-privilege permissions only for required resources.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Pipeline-as-Code (CloudFormation)
Why Pipeline-as-Code?
Version control your pipeline definitions to make them auditable and reproducible, and to enable automation when creating or updating pipelines across environments.
Best Practice
Parameterize buckets, IAM roles, and ARNs so the template can be reused in multiple accounts or environments.
CloudFormation Snippet
# CloudFormation snippet for a simple CodePipeline
Resources:
  MyWebAppPipeline:
    Type: AWS::CodePipeline::Pipeline
    Properties:
      Name: MyWebAppCI-CD
      RoleArn: !GetAtt CodePipelineServiceRole.Arn
      ArtifactStore:
        Type: S3
        Location: !Ref PipelineArtifactsBucket
      Stages:
        - Name: Source
          Actions:
            - Name: SourceCode
              ActionTypeId:
                Category: Source
                Owner: AWS
                Provider: CodeCommit
                Version: '1'
              OutputArtifacts:
                - Name: SourceOutput
              Configuration:
                RepositoryName: !Ref CodeCommitRepoName
                BranchName: master
              RunOrder: 1
        - Name: Build
          Actions:
            - Name: BuildImage
              ActionTypeId:
                Category: Build
                Owner: AWS
                Provider: CodeBuild
                Version: '1'
              InputArtifacts:
                - Name: SourceOutput
              OutputArtifacts:
                - Name: BuildOutput
              Configuration:
                ProjectName: !Ref CodeBuildProjectName
              RunOrder: 1
        - Name: Deploy
          Actions:
            - Name: DeployToECS
              ActionTypeId:
                Category: Deploy
                Owner: AWS
                Provider: CodeDeploy
                Version: '1'
              InputArtifacts:
                - Name: BuildOutput
              Configuration:
                ApplicationName: !Ref CodeDeployApplicationName
                DeploymentGroupName: !Ref CodeDeployDeploymentGroupName
              RunOrder: 1

screens.title: Monitoring, EventBridge, and Notifications
screens.narratorSegment: Monitoring pipelines is essential for fast response to failures and to keep teams informed during manual approvals. CodePipeline emits state-change events that integrate with Amazon EventBridge. You can create EventBridge rules to match pipeline started, stage failed, or action succeeded events and route them to targets like SNS topics, Lambda functions, or step functions. Use SNS for simple team notifications via email or chat, and Lambda to implement automated reactions such as cleanup or retries. For troubleshooting, rely on logs from the underlying services: CodeBuild logs appear in CloudWatch Logs, and CodeDeploy logs are on instances or in CloudWatch. Typical failures include wrong artifact names, insufficient IAM permissions for the pipeline or service roles, and misconfigured action parameters. A common error pattern is granting overly broad permissions to quickly fix a failure; instead, identify the minimal missing permission, for example iam:PassRole for passing execution roles, and add that to the service role. Key takeaway: wire EventBridge to notify teams and automate recovery, and always inspect the service-specific logs when debugging. Monitoring, EventBridge, and Notifications means use eventbridge and sns for notifications and inspect codebuild/codedeploy logs for detailed troubleshooting.. In practical terms, track pipeline state changes and alert teams for failures or approvals. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Activity Walkthrough: Static Website Pipeline with Approval
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough guides you through creating a simple pipeline that deploys a static site to S3 and includes a manual approval gate. Start with prerequisites: a CodeCommit repository containing index. html, an S3 bucket configured for static website hosting, and an IAM role for CodePipeline with permissions to access CodeCommit, S3, and CloudWatch Logs. Create an S3 artifacts bucket. For example, run the bucket creation command with the AWS CLI. Next, create the pipeline in the console or via CloudFormation: define the pipeline name, service role, artifact store, and stages. For the Source stage choose CodeCommit and point to your repository and branch. Skip the build stage for this static site; configure Deploy with an S3 deploy action targeting the website bucket and enable extract before deploy if you packaged files. After creation, add a ManualApproval stage between Source and Deploy, attach an SNS topic if you want notifications, and limit approvers via IAM. Test by committing a small change to index. html, observe the pipeline start, confirm it pauses at approval, then approve to complete the deployment. Misconception: skipping build means the deploy action must consume the correct SourceOutput artifact — configure it explicitly. Closing prompt: how would you extend this pipeline to run accessibility checks before approval?

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we’ll make AWS CodePipeline tangible. You will understand what an end-to-end pipeline is, why stages, actions, and artifacts matter, and how CodePipeline connects developer tools like CodeCommit, CodeBuild, and CodeDeploy into a reliable release flow. We’ll also cover how to pause for human checks with manual approval gates, extend behavior with custom actions backed by Lambda, and manage your pipeline safely as code using CloudFormation or CDK. Practically, you’ll see how artifacts flow from source to build to deploy, where IAM permissions commonly fail, and how EventBridge and SNS keep teams informed. This matters because a well-designed pipeline reduces deployment risk, enforces quality gates, and makes releases repeatable and auditable. By the end you’ll be able to sketch a multi-stage pipeline for container or static workloads, choose where to add tests and approvals, and pick an approach to represent the pipeline as code. Think about a recent deployment you managed: where would an approval or a custom scan fit into that process?

By the end of this chapter you will design, implement, and operate multi-stage CodePipeline workflows for different application types. First, you will learn to map release requirements to pipeline stages and actions so that source changes progress through build, test, and deploy steps reliably. Second, you will integrate AWS developer tools—CodeCommit for source control, CodeBuild for builds and tests, and CodeDeploy for deployments—and understand when to call out to S3, Lambda, or Step Functions. Third, you will add control points such as manual approval gates and custom actions so compliance checks and bespoke automation fit into your workflow. Finally, you will author pipelines as code with CloudFormation or CDK, enabling version control, repeatable creation, and predictable updates. Each objective links skill to outcome: for example, defining a manual approval before production reduces risk and provides an audit trail; expressing the pipeline in CloudFormation ensures the exact pipeline configuration can be recreated. Keep an eye out for common pitfalls, like misconfigured artifact names or overbroad IAM permissions, as we cover each objective with practical examples.

This page makes the assessment focus explicit and highlights common mistakes to avoid. You will be expected to produce a pipeline design that demonstrates correct artifact flows between stages, a working example that integrates CodeCommit, CodeBuild, and a deploy provider, and a pipeline-as-code template that can be deployed. We will check that manual approval actions pause and notify teams, and that any custom actions correctly communicate success or failure back to CodePipeline. Common errors include mismatched artifact names between actions, missing iam:PassRole or service role permissions, and misconfigured action provider parameters. When we review your pipeline-as-code, we will look for explicit artifact stores, a defined service role for the pipeline, and stage definitions for Source, Build, and Deploy at minimum. A short hands-on activity demonstrates a static website pipeline with a manual approval gate; successful completion shows artifacts flowing to S3 and a paused approval step that requires a human to continue. These checks ensure reproducibility, least-privilege IAM posture, and a clear audit trail for production changes.

AWS CodePipeline is a fully managed continuous delivery service that automates release pipelines, turning a set of discrete tasks into an orchestrated workflow. Think of CodePipeline as a conveyor belt in a factory: stages are inspection stations and actions are the tools that operate on the product. The Source stage places code onto the belt, Build transforms it into artifacts, Test verifies quality, and Deploy places the finished product into an environment. This conveyor analogy helps you decide where to insert quality gates: tests, manual reviews, or custom checks. A concrete example: a commit in CodeCommit triggers a Source action that produces an artifact; CodeBuild consumes that artifact to run unit tests and build a Docker image, producing a build artifact that the Deploy stage consumes to update an ECS service. A common misconception is to treat CodePipeline as a build system — it is an orchestration layer; the heavy lifting of builds and tests is delegated to CodeBuild or external tools. Key takeaway: use CodePipeline to model the high-level flow and choose specialized providers for execution. How would you break a complex release into stages so failures fail fast and tests are meaningful?

A CodePipeline is composed of stages and each stage contains actions. Stages represent logical checkpoints like Source, Build, Test, Approval, and Deploy. Actions are specific tasks within those stages — for example, a CodeCommit Source action, a CodeBuild action that runs unit tests and builds artifacts, and a CodeDeploy action that updates an ECS service. One strong design principle is to place fast, failing tests earlier, so failures are detected quickly and cost is minimized. For containerized apps, build produces a Docker image and pushes it to ECR; the build stage should also run unit tests and static analysis. An integration test stage can deploy to a short-lived staging environment and run end-to-end tests before approval. A common mistake is grouping too many responsibilities into a single stage; instead, split concerns so rollbacks and troubleshooting are easier. Concrete example: Source produces SourceOutput, Build consumes SourceOutput and produces BuildOutput; configure action artifact names explicitly so the next stage can find the right input. Check your artifact names and run order when pipelines fail to transition artifacts. Closing takeaway: structure stages to enforce fast feedback, clear ownership, and reliable artifact handoff.

Integrating AWS developer tools gives each component a clear responsibility in the pipeline. CodeCommit is the source provider; it triggers a Source action and supplies the initial artifact. CodeBuild is a build and test engine: compile code, run unit tests, produce build artifacts or container images and push to ECR. CodeDeploy is the deployment orchestrator for compute targets like EC2, ECS, or Lambda — it interprets artifacts and performs the actual switch to new versions, including blue/green strategies. A useful way to reason about them is to compare responsibilities: CodeCommit owns change tracking, CodeBuild owns transformation and verification, and CodeDeploy owns release mechanics. Concrete example: for a Docker-based microservice, CodeBuild builds the image and pushes to ECR, then produces a BuildOutput artifact containing the image tag; CodeDeploy reads that and performs a blue/green deployment to ECS. Common misconception: expecting CodePipeline to perform image builds itself; instead, configure CodeBuild with a buildspec to produce the image and artifact metadata. Key takeaway: pick the right provider for each action and make their contracts — artifacts and IAM permissions — explicit so the pipeline runs securely and predictably.

Artifacts are the outputs that actions produce and that subsequent actions consume. In CodePipeline, an artifact can be source code archive, build outputs, or metadata like image tags. The ArtifactStore, often an S3 bucket, is the durable place where artifacts are stored between stages. A clear artifact naming convention is essential: specify InputArtifacts and OutputArtifacts in each action so the pipeline can route files correctly. For example, a Source action writes SourceOutput; a subsequent CodeBuild action lists SourceOutput in InputArtifacts and writes BuildOutput to OutputArtifacts. If an action cannot find its expected artifact, the pipeline fails to transition. A common mistake is forgetting to set the artifact name when skipping build stages or when using multiple actions producing different outputs. Practically, when building a static website pipeline, SourceOutput should contain index. html and BuildOutput can be skipped if no build is required; configure the Deploy action to extract files from SourceOutput. Key takeaway: artifacts and the artifact store are the contract between actions — define names and stores explicitly to avoid handoff errors. Artifacts and Artifact Stores means treat artifacts and the artifact store as explicit contracts between actions; name them clearly and use s3 as the durable store.. In practical terms, how artifacts travel between actions and the role of s3. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Beyond the core developer tools, CodePipeline integrates well with S3, Lambda, and Step Functions to handle artifact storage, custom logic, and long-running orchestration. Use S3 as an artifact store and also as a deploy target for static websites. AWS Lambda commonly implements custom actions: a Lambda function can run a proprietary security scan, manipulate artifacts, or emit success and failure back to CodePipeline. Step Functions are useful when a pipeline needs to coordinate a sequence of longer-running tasks or multiple Lambda calls as part of a single logical action. For example, a SecurityScan stage might invoke a Step Functions workflow that executes several scanners and aggregates results; that workflow can then return status to CodePipeline via a custom action. A common misconception is to overuse Lambda for heavy compute; keep Lambdas lightweight and prefer CodeBuild or Step Functions for heavier workloads. When integrating these services, define clear input and output contracts and ensure the pipeline role and any invoked roles have least-privilege permissions. Takeaway: use S3 for durable artifacts, Lambda for short custom actions, and Step Functions when you need orchestrated, multi-step custom logic.

Manual approval gates insert human judgment into an automated pipeline. You add an Approval action in a stage and when the pipeline reaches that action it pauses until an authorized user reviews and approves or rejects progression. Approvals are essential for production deployments, compliance checks, and high-risk releases. In practice you pair an approval action with SNS notifications so the right people know a review is required and have links to artifacts or logs to make their decision. A concrete example: after an integration test stage you add a ManualApproval action that references an SNS topic; reviewers receive a notification, examine test reports or artifacts, and then approve the pipeline to proceed to production. Misconception: approvals are not a substitute for automated tests — they are complementary and should follow meaningful automated validation so reviewers are not forced to manually validate trivial failures. Practical tip: limit who can approve by IAM and include a clear review checklist in the approval message. Closing question to reflect on: which release types in your organization require manual approval, and what evidence should reviewers see before approving?

Custom actions let you plug functionality into a pipeline that CodePipeline does not natively support. To build a custom action you define an action type and implement the action logic, typically in a Lambda function or an agent running on EC2. The custom action must communicate back to CodePipeline by calling PutJobSuccessResult or PutJobFailureResult so the pipeline knows whether to proceed. A practical scenario is a proprietary security scanner: you might have a SecurityScan stage that uses a custom action; the Lambda invokes the scanner, waits for results, then signals pass or fail. A common pitfall is not handling timeouts or long-running scans: if the scan takes minutes, ensure the Lambda design or execution model supports waiting or that Step Functions are used to orchestrate extended work. Misconception: custom actions are a free-form replacement for tests — they are best used when a tool cannot be integrated as a standard provider. Key takeaway: implement clear success/failure signaling and robust error handling in custom actions, and ensure the pipeline role and any invoked roles have only the permissions required for the task.

Remember these core ideas as you design pipelines. First, CodePipeline is an orchestration layer: it models stages and actions while delegating actual work to providers like CodeBuild and CodeDeploy. Second, artifacts are contracts: name InputArtifacts and OutputArtifacts explicitly and use an S3 artifact store so actions can reliably find the files they need. Third, approvals and custom actions are powerful controls: use Manual Approval for high-risk production steps and implement custom actions with Lambda or Step Functions when you must integrate tools not offered as native providers. Keep these three concepts in mind and you will build reliable, auditable pipelines that match both developer velocity and operational controls.
